Inflation. The general and sustained increase in the price level of goods and services in an economy over time. Inflation is measured as a percentage rate per year. Three percent inflation means the average price of a bundle of goods rises by three percent in a year. Inflation erodes the purchasing power of money. One hundred dollars today buys less next year if inflation is positive.

Moderate inflation, around one to three percent, is often considered healthy and compatible with steady growth. High inflation above five to ten percent creates uncertainty and distorts economic decisions. Deflation, negative inflation, is rare in modern economies but economically damaging. It traps consumers and firms in a cycle of deferred spending, making problems worse.

Inflation is measured through indices. The Consumer Price Index tracks price changes in a basket of goods and services bought by households. The Producer Price Index tracks prices at the wholesale level. Core inflation excludes volatile items like food and energy to reveal underlying inflationary pressure.

What causes inflation? Demand-pull inflation occurs when too much money chases too few goods. Aggregate demand exceeds aggregate supply, often in booms. Cost-push inflation results from rising production costs like wages or oil prices. Monetary inflation comes from rapid growth in the money supply without corresponding growth in output.

Inflation has winners and losers. Borrowers win because they repay loans with devalued currency. Firms that can raise prices quickly win. Savers lose as their savings lose purchasing power. Creditors lose. Workers with fixed wages lose. Moderate inflation is often accepted as the cost of full employment. It encourages spending and investment. High inflation creates uncertainty and erodes real wages. It can trigger wage-price spirals where workers demand higher wages, firms raise prices, and the cycle continues.

The Phillips Curve describes the trade-off between low unemployment, which raises inflation, and low inflation, which requires accepting higher unemployment. After decades of mostly low inflation following the nineteen eighties, the surge above five to eight percent from two thousand twenty-one to twenty twenty-three forced central banks to aggressively raise interest rates. Understanding inflation is essential to understanding monetary policy and why savers and borrowers have opposite preferences about inflation.
